paragraphs: BetterV addresses automated circuit design through Verilog, a language used to describe hardware. The paper combines specialized language-model training with guidance aimed at particular design requirements. This brings two objectives into the same framework: producing correct hardware descriptions and improving how those descriptions perform in downstream electronic design tools.

The training pipeline collects Verilog modules from the internet, filters and processes them, and uses specially designed instruction tuning to teach the model Verilog knowledge. Data augmentation expands the training material. The augmented data also supports task-specific generative discriminators, which guide generation toward implementations suited to a chosen design objective.

The authors report that BetterV generates syntactically and functionally correct Verilog and outperforms GPT-4 on VerilogEval. Discriminator guidance also improves downstream tasks, including reducing synthesis netlist nodes and shortening verification runtime with Boolean satisfiability solving. These findings connect code-generation quality to concrete hardware-design outcomes: the framework evaluates usefulness beyond whether generated text resembles valid Verilog.
icml-2024-betterv-controlled-verilog-gen.tldr: BetterV combines Verilog instruction tuning with task-specific discriminator guidance to improve hardware-code correctness and downstream design outcomes.

paragraphs: Neural networks can fit every training example and still predict well on unseen data, even when they have many more parameters than seem necessary. This paper examines two explanations: the network architecture may favor useful solutions, or stochastic gradient descent may preferentially find them. Separating these effects requires looking beyond training accuracy alone.

The authors compare random networks and networks optimized by stochastic gradient descent, considering networks that achieve zero training error. They vary width and depth to distinguish different forms of overparameterization. Because both groups fit the training data, differences in generalization help reveal whether the optimization procedure or the architecture accounts for the observed behavior.

In experiments with few training samples, increasing width improves generalization through the bias of stochastic gradient descent, rather than an architectural bias. Increasing depth instead hurts generalization, with random and optimized networks behaving similarly; the authors attribute this effect to architecture. These findings make the low-sample setting and the distinction between width and depth central to interpreting overparameterization.
icml-2024-bias-of-stochastic-gradient-de.tldr: In low-sample experiments, wider networks benefit from SGD’s bias, while greater depth harms generalization through an architectural effect.

paragraphs: Optimizing several competing objectives means searching for useful tradeoffs. Multi-objective Bayesian optimization chooses which candidate to evaluate next through an acquisition function. Some existing acquisition functions become computationally expensive as the number of objectives grows because they integrate over the space of possible objective values.

The paper connects non-dominated solutions, which cannot be improved in one objective without sacrificing another, to the highest multivariate rank. This rank corresponds to an extreme level line of the joint cumulative distribution function. Using that connection, the authors introduce a CDF indicator for assessing approximate Pareto sets. The indicator respects Pareto comparisons and can complement the widely used hypervolume indicator.

BOtied turns this indicator into an acquisition function. It uses copulas, statistical tools for representing dependence across variables, to support efficient implementation with many objectives. Experiments on synthetic and real-world problems report better performance than state-of-the-art multi-objective Bayesian optimization methods while remaining computationally efficient. The contribution therefore links a new way to assess tradeoff sets with a practical rule for directing the search.
icml-2024-botied-multi-objective-bayesia.tldr: BOtied uses multivariate ranks and a CDF-based quality indicator to guide efficient Bayesian optimization across many competing objectives.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a model perform a task using information supplied in its input, without updating its parameters. This paper asks how well state-space models, particularly Mamba, support that ability compared with Transformers. The question matters because these models offer alternatives to the quadratic computational cost associated with multi-head attention.

The study compares the architectures across several kinds of in-context learning tasks. State-space models perform similarly to Transformers on standard regression tasks and better on tasks such as sparse parity learning. However, they perform worse when tasks require non-standard retrieval. This pattern shows that competitive performance on one form of contextual learning does not establish equally strong performance across other task requirements.

The authors introduce MambaFormer, a hybrid architecture combining Mamba with attention blocks. It surpasses the individual architectures on tasks where they struggle independently. The results support hybrid designs as a promising direction for improving in-context learning: different sequence-processing mechanisms can contribute useful capabilities within one model, with the observed advantages depending on the task.
icml-2024-can-mamba-learn-how-to-learn-a.tldr: Mamba’s in-context learning strengths vary by task, and combining it with attention improves performance where individual architectures struggle.

paragraphs: This paper approaches neural-network compression by changing how interactions between neurons are represented. In the authors’ physics-inspired view, a network is a dynamic system. Conventional descriptions use weighted linear interactions and obtain nonlinearity from activation functions; the paper argues that this arrangement limits the model’s overall nonlinear representation and data-fitting ability.

The proposed RieM method draws on Riemannian geometry. It places neurons in a Riemannian state space and describes their interactions using a metric on that space. The authors use this formulation to build a more parameter-efficient neural representation and then a compression mechanism that does not require additional fine-tuning with real data.

Experiments include ResNet and Vision Transformer backbones, with evaluations on MNIST, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1k, and COCO object detection. At equal compression rates and computational complexity, RieM-compressed models achieve higher inference accuracy than existing data-free compression methods. The reported advantage concerns how much predictive performance the compressed representation retains under matched resource conditions, making the geometry-based interaction model relevant to practical model compression.
icml-2024-data-free-neural-representatio.tldr: RieM uses geometry-based neuronal interactions to compress networks without real-data fine-tuning, improving accuracy over compared data-free methods at matched resource levels.

paragraphs: E-commerce models must support varied tasks and cope with products or requests outside their training experience. The paper identifies limited generalist capability and weak out-of-domain performance as problems for conventional approaches. It explores whether instruction-tuned language models can provide a more broadly useful foundation for e-commerce applications.

The authors construct ECInstruct, an openly available, large-scale instruction dataset for e-commerce, described as the first of its kind. They use it to instruction-tune general-purpose language models, producing the eCeLLM model family. The dataset and models form a combined contribution: domain-focused instructions provide the training material for adapting general language capabilities to e-commerce tasks.

In the reported in-domain evaluations, eCeLLM substantially outperforms the compared baselines, including GPT-4 and state-of-the-art task-specific models. It also generalizes well to unseen products and unseen instructions. These findings support its proposed role as a generalist e-commerce model across the evaluated settings. Public availability of both ECInstruct and eCeLLM makes the training resource and resulting models accessible for further work.
icml-2024-ecellm-generalizing-large-lang.tldr: eCeLLM uses the ECInstruct dataset to adapt language models for e-commerce, reporting strong in-domain results and generalization to unseen products and instructions.

paragraphs: This paper develops a satellite-based framework for estimating canopy height at global scale. A central challenge is the reliability of the height measurements used as ground-truth labels. Their locations can be inaccurate, and mountainous terrain can introduce erroneous labels. The framework addresses these issues as part of producing more dependable height predictions.

The approach combines advanced preprocessing with a new loss function designed to counter geolocation inaccuracies in the reference measurements. It also uses Shuttle Radar Topography Mission data to filter erroneous labels in mountainous regions. These components make the quality and spatial alignment of training information central to the estimation pipeline.

Against ground-truth labels, the reported overall mean absolute error is 2.43 meters and root mean squared error is 4.73 meters. For trees taller than five meters, those errors are 4.45 and 6.72 meters, respectively. The authors report substantial improvement over existing global-scale products. The resulting map and framework are intended to support global ecological analysis, including large-scale forest and biomass monitoring.
icml-2024-estimating-canopy-height-at-sc.tldr: A satellite-based canopy-height framework addresses location errors and unreliable mountain labels, reporting improved accuracy over existing global-scale products.

paragraphs: Program analysis requires understanding what code does, including when different forms of code preserve the same meaning. This paper uses those meaning-preserving transformations as architectural structure for learning program semantics. It formalizes them as code symmetries and organizes them into a group, providing a mathematical basis for reasoning about equivalent program forms.

The proposed model, SymC, introduces a self-attention mechanism that is provably equivariant to code symmetries from a permutation group defined over the program dependence graph. Equivariance means that applying an allowed transformation to the input produces a corresponding transformation in the model’s representation. This builds the specified structural relationship directly into how the model processes code.

Across five program-analysis tasks, SymC outperforms state-of-the-art code models, including GPT-4, without pre-training. The authors interpret these results as evidence that encoding program structure through code symmetry groups can improve the speed and quality of generalization. The contribution combines a mathematical guarantee about the attention mechanism with empirical evidence of its usefulness for the evaluated analysis tasks.
icml-2024-exploiting-code-symmetries-for.tldr: SymC builds meaning-preserving code symmetries into self-attention and outperforms compared code models on five program-analysis tasks without pre-training.

paragraphs: This paper tackles how to pre-train general-purpose reinforcement-learning policies from unlabeled offline experience. Existing approaches can restrict behavioral diversity, depend on strong demonstrations, or leave downstream adaptation unclear. The proposed framework aims to capture diverse, optimal behaviors over long horizons and make them available for new tasks through zero-shot adaptation.

Its central idea is to learn a structured representation that preserves the environment’s temporal structure. Policies then learn directional movements spanning this representation space. Those directions provide a way to prompt the policy for downstream behavior, connecting the organization of the learned space to mechanisms for selecting actions appropriate to a task.

Experiments on simulated robotic locomotion and manipulation show that the pre-trained policies solve both goal-conditioned and general reinforcement-learning tasks without further task-specific training. They often outperform earlier methods tailored to the individual settings. These results support the usefulness of temporal representations and directional policy prompting for the evaluated tasks, while the broader framework is designed to enable adaptation to arbitrary new tasks.
icml-2024-foundation-policies-with-hilbe.tldr: Hilbert representations organize offline experience into directional behaviors that can be prompted to solve downstream reinforcement-learning tasks without additional training.

paragraphs: Graph-based data has structure in the relationships between vertices. This paper argues that treating every permutation of vertices as a symmetry overlooks those relationships. For a particular graph, the relevant symmetries are its automorphisms: vertex rearrangements that preserve the graph’s structure. The goal is to build neural networks that respect precisely this group.

The authors fully characterize the learnable linear functions that are equivariant to a graph’s automorphism group between layers formed from tensor powers of the vertex-coordinate space. Equivariance requires transforming the input and then applying the layer to agree with applying the layer and transforming its output. They provide a spanning set of matrices that describes these allowable linear layer functions.

This characterization supplies concrete building blocks for networks whose symmetry matches a given graph. Its theoretical reach extends to data with any finite symmetry group: an established theorem states that every finite group is isomorphic to some graph’s automorphism group. The paper therefore connects graph-specific layer construction with a broader framework for finite-group-equivariant learning.
icml-2024-graph-automorphism-group-equiv.tldr: The paper characterizes linear neural-network layers that respect a graph’s actual automorphisms, with implications for learning under any finite symmetry group.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning seeks to remove the influence of particular training examples. Fully retraining a large language model is computationally impractical, while many approximate methods require access to model parameters. This paper considers a different access pattern: changing the information supplied to the model at inference time, without updating its weights.

The proposed in-context unlearning method places the instances to be unlearned into the input context alongside labels that differ from their correct labels. These examples become the mechanism for altering the model’s responses. The method therefore makes the inference-time context the point of intervention, addressing situations where computational constraints or query-only access prevent parameter updates.

Experiments show performance comparable to, and sometimes better than, state-of-the-art unlearning methods that require parameter access. The authors report reduced influence of the selected instances while preserving test accuracy. These are empirical findings about the proposed contextual intervention. The contribution is an alternative route to unlearning behavior that operates through supplied inputs and expands the range of access conditions under which unlearning methods can be applied.
icml-2024-in-context-unlearning-language.tldr: In-context unlearning uses deliberately relabeled examples at inference time to reduce selected training instances’ influence without changing model parameters.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers information from a teacher model to a student by aligning their predictive distributions. The paper argues that using the same distribution-modeling strategy for both can make this transfer suboptimal because their capacities differ. Adapting the teacher to the student can help, but may require complicated or student-specific training procedures.

The authors instead introduce an auxiliary variable related to the prediction targets. They use it to reformulate the student’s predictive distribution and derive a new distillation objective. This changes how the student represents the predictive information it is learning, aiming to increase its ability to model that information despite the capacity gap.

The paper provides theoretical insights into why the resulting objective can outperform existing distillation objectives. Its experiments report considerable and consistent improvements over existing methods. Together, the analysis and evaluations support the auxiliary variable as a useful way to improve knowledge transfer. The key contribution is the reformulated learning objective, which addresses the teacher–student mismatch through the student’s predictive modeling.
icml-2024-knowledge-distillation-with-au.tldr: An auxiliary variable reshapes the student’s predictive distribution to improve knowledge distillation across teacher–student capacity differences.

paragraphs: A controller often needs to reach a desired state and keep the system nearby indefinitely. This stability requirement becomes especially important when states can grow without bound. In a queueing network, for example, a stable policy keeps queues finite, while an optimal policy additionally minimizes their lengths.

The paper finds that deep reinforcement-learning methods trained online to minimize distance from the desired state often produce unstable policies. Although an optimal policy would be stable, the learning process does not reliably reach that behavior. The authors attribute the problem to poor credit assignment: training does not adequately connect destabilizing actions with their consequences.

Their approach combines Lyapunov-based cost shaping with transformations of the unbounded state space. These changes address the learning signal and the state representation together. Experiments on queueing networks and traffic-signal control find competitive performance against strong baselines that know the transition dynamics. The results support addressing stability explicitly in the learning setup when directly optimizing proximity to the desired state yields policies that drift away.
icml-2024-learning-to-stabilize-online-r.tldr: Lyapunov-based cost shaping and state transformations help online reinforcement learning address unstable behavior in systems with unbounded states.

paragraphs: A machine-learning architecture can contain a layer that solves a parameterized optimization problem. Such layers provide useful structure, but training the surrounding model can be difficult. Their derivatives may be degenerate, leaving stochastic gradient descent with information that does not meaningfully indicate how to improve the model.

Lagrangian Proximal Gradient Descent, or LPGD, replaces these uninformative derivatives with meaningful training signals. It does so by running the existing forward optimization solver again on a perturbed input. The framework integrates with automatic differentiation libraries, allowing the solver-based replacement to participate in backpropagation through the larger architecture.

The authors show that several previously proposed methods fit within LPGD as special cases and establish connections to traditional optimization methods. They also analyze the framework theoretically. Experiments on historical and synthetic data show faster convergence than gradient descent, even in a differentiable setup. This last result suggests that the approach can be useful beyond cases where degenerate derivatives make ordinary gradient information ineffective.
icml-2024-lpgd-a-general-framework-for-b.tldr: LPGD reruns embedded optimization solvers on perturbed inputs to supply useful backpropagation signals and reports faster convergence than gradient descent.

paragraphs: LasF explores a language-modeling module inspired by neuronal behavior. It represents language tokens as functionals of semantic fields: token representations are formulated in relation to those fields. The paper describes the module as a nonlinear approximator designed for sequential data, motivated by the size and depth often required by Transformer models.

The authors first replace the final layers of pre-trained language models with LasF modules. On standard reading-comprehension and question-answering tasks, these modified models consistently achieve higher accuracy with fewer parameters. This evaluates whether the proposed representation can improve an existing model while reducing its parameter requirements.

A fully tuned LasF-based model also exceeds the previous best ensemble and single-model results on the CommonsenseQA blind test set by the reported margins of 0.4% and 3.1%, respectively. Separately, a LasF-only model trained from scratch outperforms existing parameter-efficient language models on datasets including WikiText103 and PennTreebank. The findings support both replacing portions of pre-trained models and using the module as the basis of a language model trained independently.
icml-2024-modeling-language-tokens-as-fu.tldr: LasF models tokens through semantic fields, improving reported language-task accuracy with fewer parameters and supporting models trained from scratch.

paragraphs: Deeper graph neural networks face oversmoothing and oversquashing: useful distinctions can fade, and information traveling across the graph can become difficult to preserve. This paper identifies information loss from heterophily mixing as the root cause of these issues. In the authors’ account, aggregation mixes messages carrying different category meanings and loses useful semantic distinctions.

The proposed multi-track graph convolutional network separates messages according to their category semantics and propagates them independently. Keeping these information streams apart is intended to prevent heterophilic mixing during message passing. The resulting scheme is designed to improve long-distance information flow and the conditions for maintaining separation between categories.

Empirical evaluations report state-of-the-art performance on several graph datasets and effective mitigation of both oversmoothing and oversquashing. The model reaches 86.4% accuracy on Cora, which the paper presents as a new benchmark. These results support the proposed connection between semantic separation during aggregation and stronger graph learning, with the multi-track architecture translating that explanation into a concrete message-passing method.
icml-2024-multi-track-message-passing-ta.tldr: Multi-track message passing separates category-specific information to address oversmoothing and oversquashing, reporting strong graph-learning results.

paragraphs: This paper studies how ridge regularization should be tuned when the test distribution differs from the training distribution. It considers both covariate shifts and changes in the regression relationship. The central question is how these shifts alter the best regularization level and the prediction risk achieved after optimal tuning.

The authors establish conditions determining whether the optimal regularization level is positive or negative. These conditions depend on how covariance and signal structures align across training and test data. Negative regularization can be optimal even with isotropic training features or an underparameterized design, revealing behavior that differs sharply from familiar in-distribution settings.

They also prove that optimally tuned risk is monotonic in the data aspect ratio, including when tuning permits negative regularization. The results generally require moment bounds but impose no other modeling assumptions on the training or test distributions. By allowing arbitrary distribution shifts and a broad range of regularization levels, the analysis clarifies why conclusions about optimal ridge tuning can change when prediction moves beyond the training distribution.
icml-2024-optimal-ridge-regularization-f.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal ridge regularization under distribution shifts, including conditions where negative regularization is best.

paragraphs: Changing a face or body does not remove every identifying clue from an image. Locations, objects, and distinctive attributes can still reveal information. This paper examines image anonymity through human perception, arguing that evaluations centered on detection and re-identification can overlook privacy vulnerabilities elsewhere in the image.

The authors curate a dataset for assessing anonymized images and introduce PerceptAnon, a learned metric trained with human annotations. It can evaluate an original image together with its anonymized version or assess an anonymized image alone. Its assessment includes both the subject and the surrounding context, reflecting the broader information people may use when judging anonymity.

The study treats perceived anonymity as a spectrum and discusses its implications for privacy assessment in the context of GDPR. Its contribution is a dataset and measurement approach aligned with human judgments, extending assessment beyond locally modified identifying features. The authors position this work as a foundation for further research into how image anonymization should be understood and evaluated.
icml-2024-perceptanon-exploring-the-huma.tldr: PerceptAnon learns human judgments of image anonymity while considering identifying information in both subjects and their surroundings.

paragraphs: This position paper asks why robots cannot routinely learn a newly assigned task with little human involvement. Reinforcement learning transferred from simulation to reality has achieved impressive robotic performance, yet preparing a task for learning still requires substantial human work. The authors identify this preparation as a primary obstacle to broader deployment.

They call the work environment shaping: choosing the observations available to the agent, its actions, its rewards, and the simulation dynamics. Their argument is grounded in the observation that practitioners often adjust these environment parameters to obtain a useful controller, rather than tuning the reinforcement-learning algorithm itself.

The paper advocates directing policy-optimization advances and other research toward automating these choices. It presents this as a necessary focus for scaling reinforcement learning across diverse robotic tasks. This is a research position about where effort should go: the authors argue that reducing the human labor involved in constructing learnable environments is central to making the vision of largely autonomous robot training practical.
icml-2024-position-automatic-environment.tldr: The authors argue that scaling robotic reinforcement learning requires automating the design of observations, actions, rewards, and simulation dynamics.

paragraphs: Learning what someone wants from comparisons between examples leaves a useful question unanswered: which features explain their choice? This paper approaches preference learning as a form of communication in which people use context to express what matters. Its goal is to extract finer detail from human feedback to learn a reward model, a representation of how desirable different behaviors are.

The proposed method enriches preference queries with two kinds of input: comparisons between objects and indications of which features of an example are preferable. The authors derive a learning approach that handles both users who explicitly identify features relevant to reward and users who do not. This makes the reasons behind a preference part of the learning signal.

Evaluations in linear bandit settings cover visual and language domains. The reported results support faster convergence to accurate rewards using fewer comparisons than feedback consisting only of example-level labels. A behavioral experiment involving mushroom foraging also supports real-world applicability. Together, these findings suggest that asking about preferred features can make reward learning more efficient while helping it reflect users’ preferences.
icml-2024-pragmatic-feature-preferences-.tldr: Asking people which features they prefer alongside example comparisons can help learn accurate reward models with fewer comparisons.

paragraphs: Distributed learning divides training across workers, but sending their gradients to a central server can create substantial communication costs. SignSGD reduces this burden by transmitting gradient signs and combining them through majority voting. Its convergence can deteriorate when adversarial workers manipulate their data or updates.

The paper proposes signSGD with federated defense, which aggregates signs using weights obtained through gradient sign decoding. A distinctive feature is that it uses information sent by adversarial workers with appropriate weighting. The method therefore seeks useful aggregate information even when some messages originate from compromised participants.

The authors show that convergence speed can remain invariant provided honest workers supplying trustworthy updates outnumber adversarial workers. This majority condition is essential to the stated result. Experiments across several adversarial attack scenarios report better convergence rates than traditional algorithms. The theoretical and empirical contributions together support weighted sign decoding as a way to retain communication efficiency while improving training behavior in the presence of adversarial workers.
icml-2024-signsgd-with-federated-defense.tldr: SignSGD-FD weights decoded gradient signs, allowing convergence rates to remain invariant when trustworthy honest workers outnumber adversarial workers.

paragraphs: This paper designs state-space models through their transfer functions, an alternative representation in the frequency domain. That formulation yields a sequence-parallel inference algorithm described as state-free. Increasing the state size does not impose significant additional memory or computational cost on this inference procedure, addressing a key scaling concern.

The proposed parameterization allows the spectrum of the corresponding convolutional kernel to be computed directly with a single Fast Fourier Transform. This connects the model’s mathematical representation to an efficient computational path. The efficiency comes from properties of the transfer-function formulation used to carry out sequence processing.

Across multiple sequence lengths and state sizes on Long Range Arena, experiments report an average training-speed improvement of 35% over time-domain S4 layers. The method also achieves state-of-the-art downstream performance among compared attention-free approaches. In language modeling, introducing the transfer-function parameterization improves perplexity over a long-convolution Hyena baseline. These findings link the representation change to both computational gains and stronger predictive results in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-state-free-inference-of-state-.tldr: A transfer-function parameterization enables state-free sequence processing and reports faster training and improved performance on sequence-modeling benchmarks.

paragraphs: Average-reward reinforcement learning evaluates performance over continued interaction. Global convergence results for policy-gradient methods can require advance knowledge of mixing time: how long a fixed policy’s Markov chain needs to approach its stationary distribution. Estimating this quantity is difficult in large state spaces and can lead to impractically long trajectories for gradient estimation.

The paper studies Multi-level Actor-Critic, or MAC, which uses a Multi-level Monte Carlo gradient estimator. The approach alleviates the need for oracle knowledge of mixing time in establishing global convergence for average-reward decision processes. This targets a gap between theoretical requirements and information realistically available during learning.

The analysis retains a dependence proportional to the square root of mixing time, matching the tightest dependence available from prior work. Thus, avoiding advance knowledge does not mean the process’s mixing behavior stops affecting the result. In a two-dimensional grid-world navigation experiment, MAC outperforms the existing state-of-the-art policy-gradient method for the average-reward setting, providing a concrete empirical demonstration alongside the convergence analysis.
icml-2024-towards-global-optimality-for-.tldr: MAC uses multilevel gradient estimation to alleviate mixing-time oracle requirements while retaining strong mixing-time dependence in average-reward convergence analysis.

paragraphs: Text-to-image systems may screen both prompts and generated images to prevent inappropriate outputs. UPAM examines the robustness of this combined defense through an attack framework aimed at both textual filters and visual checkers. This broadens the target beyond approaches that primarily try to bypass screening of the input text.

The framework supports gradient-based optimization. A central obstacle is that defenses may prevent the system from returning any result, leaving the optimization process without its usual output feedback. The authors introduce Sphere-Probing Learning to support gradient optimization in that situation. They also add Semantic-Enhancing Learning to refine the framework toward images aligned with the intended target.

The paper reports that UPAM maintains attack stealthiness and that extensive experiments demonstrate effectiveness and efficiency. Its main contribution is the combination of dual-defense targeting, optimization under blocked feedback, and semantic alignment. These components address distinct obstacles in evaluating whether a protected generation system can still produce target-aligned outputs despite screening at both the textual and visual stages.
icml-2024-upam-unified-prompt-attack-in-.tldr: UPAM evaluates text-to-image defenses with a unified attack framework targeting both prompt filters and image checkers, including when defenses suppress feedback.

paragraphs: Amortized variational inference produces fast approximate posteriors for new observations, but those approximations often come with few quality guarantees. CANVI adds a conformal procedure that constructs regions with a user-chosen probability of containing the truth. Its guarantee is marginal coverage, describing coverage across the relevant collection of cases rather than a separate guarantee for each observation.

Given several candidate posterior approximators, CANVI constructs conformalized predictors from each and compares their predictive efficiency. It returns the most efficient predictor while retaining the stated coverage guarantee. The procedure does not depend on particular design choices for the candidate approximators and only requires samples from the forward model, allowing use when likelihoods are unavailable.

The authors prove lower bounds on predictive efficiency and examine how posterior approximation quality relates to the efficiency of the resulting regions. Experiments on simulation-based inference benchmarks and galaxy emission spectra demonstrate accurate calibration and high predictive efficiency. The contribution connects fast approximate inference with guaranteed coverage while also comparing how efficiently candidate models produce useful prediction regions.
icml-2024-variational-inference-with-cov.tldr: CANVI converts approximate posteriors into prediction regions with guaranteed marginal coverage and selects among candidates by predictive efficiency.
